tagline: Social graphics at the right size, from a template, in about ninety seconds.
verdictSummary: Snappa exists because a general design tool is too much tool for making a Twitter header. Every design starts from a size preset, text auto-fits its box, and there is no layer panel to get lost in. Building that constrained editor is more work than it looks — auto-fitting text across a resize, and re-laying a design out when the canvas changes shape, are the two features that make it fast and the two that take days.
coreLoopDIY: Pick a platform size, start from a small set of layouts, drop in your own image and text, and export at the exact dimensions the platform wants.
whatYouLose: the stock photo allowance included in the subscription
the template library, which is why the output looks designed
team sharing and a brand kit others can use
designs stored somewhere other than your own machine
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the templates and the stock photos are the product. An editor with no library is a blank canvas, and a blank canvas is precisely what Snappa's users are paying not to face.
notes: Fixed-size, template-first and deliberately constrained — distinct from the SVG canvas, deck-as-code and data-driven infographic angles taken by the other design entries here.
prompt:
Build a deliberately constrained graphic editor for social images. Fixed sizes, auto-fitting text, no layer panel.

Sizes: every design starts by choosing a preset — square post, portrait post, story, wide header, blog banner, and a custom size. The canvas is fixed at that size and cannot be resized freely; changing to another preset triggers the relayout described below.

Elements, and no more: background (solid, gradient, or an image with position and zoom), text box, shape (rectangle, ellipse, line), image, and icon from a local set. Elements snap to a grid and to each other, with alignment guides. No layer panel — z-order is controlled by bring-forward and send-back on the selected element, which covers every real case at this complexity.

Text auto-fit, which is the feature that makes this fast. A text box has a fixed frame and the type size scales to fill it, within a min and max the user sets. Typing more text shrinks it; deleting grows it back. Support a maximum line count after which the text truncates with a visible warning rather than overflowing. Getting this right — including with line breaks, mixed weights and a bounded aspect ratio — is most of the build.

Relayout on size change, the second hard feature. Changing preset re-maps the design onto the new canvas: elements keep their proportional position relative to the anchor they were nearest (a corner, an edge, or the centre), text boxes keep their proportional width and re-fit their type, and the background image re-crops around its declared focal point. Show a before-and-after preview and let the user accept or adjust. A design system that only works at one size is why people keep separate files per platform.

Templates: a template is a design saved with its elements marked as editable or fixed. Ship no templates; the first run walks the user through saving one from a design they made. Templates are files, so a set can be shared.

Brand: a token file with a palette, two typefaces and a logo. Every colour picker offers brand colours first.

Export: PNG at exact preset dimensions and at 2x, JPEG with a quality control, and a size readout so a platform's file-size limit is visible before upload.

Storage: designs as JSON plus referenced local assets, on disk.

Out of scope: a stock photo library, a template marketplace, collaboration, print output and CMYK, and any hosted service.

faq.q: Can I export my Snappa designs?
faq.a: As finished images, yes. There is no editable export, so designs are rebuilt — which is quick for social graphics and is mostly a matter of re-creating three or four templates you actually reuse.

Because it is the thing that turns a ninety-second task into a ten-minute one. At the complexity of a social graphic — a background, an image, two text boxes and a logo — bring-forward and send-back handle every real case, and removing the panel removes a whole category of confusion.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing to run, but the stock photos are a real gap. Snappa bundles a photo allowance; here you supply your own images or use a free photo source, which is either fine or is the reason to keep paying, depending on what you make.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Starting from something. Snappa's templates mean a non-designer produces a decent graphic on the first attempt. An empty constrained editor produces a decent graphic on the fifth attempt, and most people stop at the second.
